Arrogance is the attitude of a person who believes they are far more important, more capable, or more valuable than they actually are — and who shows this belief in a way that is offensive or dismissive to others.

Think of it this way: arrogance is not just thinking you are great. It is thinking you are so great that other people barely matter in comparison.

At the heart of arrogance are two things happening at once:

1. An inflated sense of self
An arrogant person has an exaggerated opinion of their own worth — their intelligence, status, talent, beauty, power, or importance. This opinion is usually not fully deserved, or at least not as fully deserved as they believe.

2. A dismissive attitude toward others
Because they place themselves so high, they naturally place others lower. They look down on people, treat others as inferior, and act as though the feelings, opinions, or needs of others are less important than their own.

These two things feed each other. The more a person inflates themselves, the more they shrink everyone else.
What Arrogance Looks Like in Real Life

Arrogance is not an invisible feeling — it shows. Here are the most common ways it appears in behaviour:

  • Interrupting others because they assume their point is more valuable.
  • Refusing to listen to advice, feedback, or criticism, even when it is correct and helpful.
  • Talking down to people — using a tone or language that makes the other person feel small or stupid.
  • Never admitting mistakes, because admitting a mistake would mean they are not as perfect as they believe.
  • Taking credit for shared success and giving little or no acknowledgment to others.
  • Boasting and bragging repeatedly, even when no one asked.
  • Treating rules as things that apply to other people, but not to them.
  • Expecting special treatment — being served first, listened to first, or prioritised, simply because of who they think they are.

Imagine a student who scores 80% on a test. Two reactions are possible:

Reaction A (Confident): "I did well! I'm proud of my effort, and I'll keep working hard."

Reaction B (Arrogant): "I'm obviously the most talented person in this class. The teacher's questions were poorly written anyway, and the others just aren't on my level."

Reaction B is arrogance. Notice that the arrogant person:

  • Assumes their result makes them superior to others
  • Refuses to accept any flaw (blames the teacher instead)
  • Dismisses everyone else without a fair assessment
Arrogance vs. Confidence — A Critical Difference

This is one of the most important distinctions to understand, because many people confuse the two.

Confidence says: "I believe in my abilities."
Arrogance says: "My abilities make me better than you."

A confident person can say "I'm good at this" without needing to add "...and you're not." They respect others even while respecting themselves. They can accept being wrong. They don't need to put others down to feel good about themselves.

An arrogant person, on the other hand, needs to feel above others. Their sense of self-worth depends on the comparison. They feel tall only by making others feel small.

In short: confidence is self-assurance. Arrogance is self-assurance at someone else's expense.
Arrogance vs. Pride — Another Important Distinction

Pride (in its healthy form) is a quiet satisfaction in your achievements or qualities. It is self-directed and proportionate.

Arrogance is pride that has grown out of control and turned outward — it demands that others recognize and submit to your superiority. It is also disproportionate: the belief in one's own greatness exceeds what is actually warranted.

You can be proud of your work without being arrogant. But arrogance almost always involves a distorted, exaggerated kind of pride.
Why Is Arrogance Considered a Negative Quality?

Arrogance is widely seen as a flaw for several strong reasons:

  • It damages relationships. People do not enjoy being around someone who makes them feel inferior or ignored.
  • It blocks growth. An arrogant person cannot learn from mistakes, accept good advice, or improve — because in their mind, they are already perfect enough.
  • It is often inaccurate. Arrogance frequently involves a wrong self-assessment. The person overestimates themselves.
  • It is disrespectful. Arrogance disrespects the dignity and worth of other people.
  • It creates conflict. Arrogant behaviour provokes resentment, arguments, and broken trust.
How the Word Is Used in Sentences

• "His arrogance made it impossible for anyone on the team to offer suggestions."
  • "She walked into the meeting with such arrogance that she didn't bother learning anyone's name."
  • "The arrogance of that leader eventually caused his downfall — he ignored all warnings."
  • "There is a fine line between confidence and arrogance, and he crossed it long ago."
Arrogance is the attitude of someone who thinks too highly of themselves and too little of others — and shows it.
